sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities ended a volatile week lower as a disappointing run of Big Tech earnings reignited AI-spending fears and triggered a sharp chip rout on Friday. MSCI World slipped roughly **0.5%**, with MSCI Developed Markets broadly similar and MSCI Emerging Markets ending near **1,567**. In the US the S&P 500 fell about **0.6%** to **7,580**, the Nasdaq Composite dropped roughly **2%** to around **25,437** for a third straight weekly loss, and the Dow eased **0.9%** to **51,770**, with the mega-cap MAG7 cohort leading the decline. In Europe the Euro Stoxx 50 closed near **6,131**, while across APAC Japan's Nikkei 225 ended around **63,290**, China's CSI 300 near **3,985** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng near **23,294**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities fell for a third consecutive week as a heavy slate of mega-cap earnings reignited AI-valuation fears. The S&P 500 slid about **0.6%** to **7,580** and the Nasdaq Composite dropped roughly **2%** to near **25,437**, logging its steepest single-session fall since March 2025 on Friday, while the Dow eased **0.9%** to **51,770**.

Earnings drove the moves. Intel cratered **29%** on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, after weak Q4 revenue guidance of **$15–16bn**, while Amazon slipped on a top- and bottom-line miss and Alphabet had tumbled **12%** midweek. The Magnificent Seven broke below technical support as investors rotated away from crowded AI and tech names.

Policy and data framed the week. The Fed left rates at **3.75–4.00%** in a **10–2** vote, offering little steer on a possible December move, while Q3 GDP grew a firm **3.4%** annualised, consumer confidence rose to **91.7** and jobless claims fell to **194,000**.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities proved more resilient than Wall Street, rebounding through midweek before the US technology rout clipped Friday's advance. The pan-regional STOXX Europe 600 reached a multi-week high near **649** on Thursday, up around **2%** on the week before the late pullback, with Germany's DAX close to **26,053** and France's CAC 40 around **7,970**; the Euro Stoxx 50 finished near **6,131**.

The ECB held its deposit rate at **2.50%** as expected and signalled a likely **25bp** hike in December, while confirming that President Lagarde will step down early, on 7 February 2027.

Strong corporate earnings underpinned sentiment, but luxury and globally geared technology names lagged into the close as AI-spending concerns and softer US mega-caps weighed on risk appetite, leaving pronounced sector dispersion across the region.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets were buffeted by the global technology sell-off, with losses concentrated on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell about **2.1%** to around **63,290** as the US semiconductor rout hit chip-related names, while China's CSI 300 slid roughly **1.4%** to near **3,985** amid renewed mainland-tech weakness.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng was comparatively resilient, ending near **23,294** (approx.), while broader Asia ex-Japan tracked Wall Street lower as the AI trade wobbled.

Policy was in focus as the BoJ held its policy rate steady at its 29–30 October meeting while retaining a hawkish bias. Tokyo core CPI rose **2.6%** y/y in October and the 10-year JGB yield ended little changed at **2.78%**, keeping expectations of further normalisation firmly alive.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar's reaction to robust US data was muted, with the greenback needing firmer conviction on December or January tightening to extend its rally. Rate differentials and risk sentiment dominated a week framed by three central-bank holds and looming US midterms.

The euro slid to an 18-month low around **1.1105** after a dovish ECB statement, before hawkish remarks from Lagarde helped it pare losses. Sterling outperformed, with GBP/USD climbing back above **1.34** from its early-October lows near **1.31** and reaching a fresh 18-month high against the euro.

The yen drew support from the BoJ's hawkish hold, which threatened carry trades, though still-wide US–Japan rate differentials capped its recovery and kept broader EM currencies on the back foot.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities underscored a year of dramatic sector rotation, with energy strength offsetting a slide in precious metals to leave the broad Bloomberg Commodity index little changed for October. Crude oil and diesel were supported by Middle East supply disruptions and tight refined-product markets, while European natural gas surged around **38%**.

Precious metals retreated, with silver and platinum among October's biggest losers and gold also easing after its strong run. Copper weakened on rising exchange-monitored inventories and speculation over potential US tariffs on refined imports, though structural electrification demand offered a floor.

The divergence reinforced the case for commodity diversification, with firmer energy reviving inflation-hedging interest even as growth worries and a steady dollar tempered enthusiasm across the wider complex.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign bonds rallied as the equity sell-off and a trio of central-bank holds drew demand into core government debt. The 10-year UST ended the week near **4.91%** and the 2-year around **4.56%**, its lowest in more than six weeks, well off the 10-year's early-October peak of about **5.34%**.

With the Fed on hold at **3.75–4.00%**, markets kept a December hike partly priced, while the ECB's hold at **2.50%** came with guidance for a likely **25bp** December increase; the BoJ's hawkish hold left the 10-year JGB near **2.78%**.

Credit tone softened modestly alongside the tech-led de-risking, with HY spreads widening while IG proved more resilient, aided by the flight-to-quality bid into core government bonds.
